questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q1] Which bitwise operation toggles the k-th bit of an integer variable 'num' without altering other bits?
questions.codeSnippet: num = num ^ (1 << k);
options: num = num >> k
num ^= (1 << k) (XOR with a single-bit mask).
questions.correctAnswer: num ^= (1 << k) (XOR with a single-bit mask).
questions.explanation: Bitwise XOR with 1 flips the bit (0->1, 1->0), while XOR with 0 preserves original bit state.
questions.hint: XOR with 1 toggles; OR sets; AND with NOT clears.
questions.interviewTip: Bit manipulation is evaluated in all embedded, firmware, and low-level screening rounds.

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q2] What determines the memory alignment padding inserted by modern C compilers inside structs?
options: Always strictly packs bytes with zero gaps.
Aligns member offsets to multiples of member size (e.g. 8-byte boundary for double), padding struct to a multiple of largest member.
Aligns all variables to 64-byte cache line boundaries.
Padding depends only on operating system file system block size.
questions.correctAnswer: Aligns member offsets to multiples of member size (e.g. 8-byte boundary for double), padding struct to a multiple of largest member.
questions.explanation: CPUs read words faster when aligned to natural boundaries. The double member (8 bytes) requires 8-byte offset alignment.
questions.hint: Largest member alignment constraint dictates total struct sizing.
questions.interviewTip: Arrange struct members from largest to smallest to minimize padding waste.

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q3] Why does executing '*ptr = 'Z';' on 'char *ptr = "Data";' crash with Segmentation Fault on Unix/Linux?
questions.codeSnippet:
char *ptr = "Data";
*ptr = 'Z'; // Segfault
options: Heap memory was exhausted.
Pointer was null.
Pointers to char can only hold ASCII 0-127.
String literals are placed in read-only text (.rodata) memory segment by the linker.
questions.correctAnswer: String literals are placed in read-only text (.rodata) memory segment by the linker.
questions.explanation: Modifying write-protected memory pages causes the CPU memory management unit (MMU) to trigger a segmentation violation.
questions.hint: String literals live in read-only text segments.
questions.interviewTip: Use 'char str[] = "Data";' to allocate mutable stack storage.

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q4] When evaluating pointer expression '*(arr + 3)' where 'int arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};', what value is retrieved?
options: 30 (dereferences index 2).
40 (dereferences index 3 directly).
Address of arr[3].
Garbage memory value.
questions.correctAnswer: 40 (dereferences index 3 directly).
questions.explanation: *(arr + i) is mathematically identical to arr[i]. With offset 3, it fetches the 4th element (40).
questions.hint: arr[i] is defined as *(arr + i) in standard C.
questions.interviewTip: Pointer subscript symmetry means 3[arr] is also valid C syntax!

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q5] What occurs if a function returns a pointer to a local stack array 'int local[10]' in C?
options: Stack frame is automatically preserved in heap.
Triggers a mandatory compiler abort.
Memory is promoted to static global scope.
Returns a dangling pointer to deallocated stack memory, causing undefined behavior on access.
questions.correctAnswer: Returns a dangling pointer to deallocated stack memory, causing undefined behavior on access.
questions.explanation: Stack frames are invalidated upon function return. Accessing returned stack pointers invokes undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Stack allocations are freed when function returns.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Dynamic Heap vs Stack Lifetime
questions.interviewTip: Always use malloc() or pass a buffer pointer from caller if data must outlive function execution.

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q6] What is the exact evaluation order and side-effect behavior of the expression `x = i++ + ++i;` in C when `i` is initialized to `2`?
questions.codeSnippet:
int i = 2;
int x = i++ + ++i;
options: x evaluates to 6, and i becomes 4.
Undefined Behavior due to multiple unsequenced modifications to 'i' between consecutive sequence points / sequence points rules.
x evaluates to 5, and i becomes 4.
x evaluates to 7, and i becomes 3.
questions.correctAnswer: Undefined Behavior due to multiple unsequenced modifications to 'i' between consecutive sequence points / sequence points rules.
questions.explanation: According to the C standard, between the previous and next sequence point (or sequencing rules in C11/C18), an object's value shall be modified at most once by the evaluation of an expression. In `i++ + ++i`, `i` is modified twice without an intervening sequence point, resulting in undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Check the C standard rules regarding modifying the same scalar variable multiple times without a sequence point.
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test deep knowledge of the C language specification beyond simple compiler output.

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q7] What is the primary implication of applying the 'extern' keyword to a global variable declaration inside a C source file function?
options: It forces the compiler to allocate 'counter' on the heap instead of the data segment.
It makes 'counter' thread-local storage automatically.

It informs the compiler that the variable 'counter' is defined elsewhere (either in another file or later in the same translation unit), extending its visibility locally without allocating storage inside the function.
It turns 'counter' into a constant read-only variable equivalent to 'const int'.
questions.correctAnswer: It informs the compiler that the variable 'counter' is defined elsewhere (either in another file or later in the same translation unit), extending its visibility locally without allocating storage inside the function.
questions.explanation: Using 'extern' inside a block declares a variable with linkage and informs the compiler that the storage for the variable is defined elsewhere, avoiding duplicate allocation and granting access to the linkage scope.
questions.hint: Think about storage duration, linkage, and where the compiler looks for variable symbols.
questions.interviewTip: Useful for verifying whether candidates understand how scope and linkage interact in multi-file C projects.

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q8] What is the standard-defined behavior when applying the integer division or modulo operators where either operand is negative, specifically regarding the direction of truncation in C99 and later?
questions.codeSnippet: int result = -7 / 3;
options: Truncation is always toward negative infinity (-7 / 3 results in -3)
The direction of truncation is implementation-defined
Division by negative operands results in undefined behavior
Truncation is toward zero (-7 / 3 results in -2)
questions.correctAnswer: Truncation is toward zero (-7 / 3 results in -2)
questions.explanation: Since C99, integer division in C rounds toward zero (truncation toward zero). Therefore, -7 / 3 evaluates to -2, and -7 % 3 evaluates to -1. Prior to C99, the rounding direction for negative operands was implementation-defined.
questions.hint: Think about how modern C standards mandate division rounding for negative integers relative to zero.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Integer Division and Modulo Truncation Rules
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to check if candidates know the changes introduced in the C99 standard regarding arithmetic operators.

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q9] What is the primary reason that using `printf` without a format string specifier (e.g., `printf(user_input);` where `user_input` comes from an untrusted source) constitutes a critical security vulnerability?
questions.codeSnippet:
char *user_input = "%s%s%s%s";
printf(user_input);
options: It allows format string attacks, enabling arbitrary memory read and write via specifiers like %n.
It always causes an immediate segmentation fault due to stack imbalance.
It automatically promotes all arguments to floating-point types, corrupting integer values.
It triggers a buffer overflow in the internal print stream buffer.
questions.correctAnswer: It allows format string attacks, enabling arbitrary memory read and write via specifiers like %n.
questions.explanation: Passing untrusted user data directly as the format argument to `printf` allows an attacker to use format specifiers like %x to leak stack contents or %n to write arbitrary values to memory addresses, leading to remote code execution.
questions.hint: Consider what happens when format specifiers are embedded directly inside strings passed as the first argument to variadic formatting functions.
questions.interviewTip: This tests secure coding knowledge and understanding of variadic function risks in C.

questions.question: [C • Test 1 • Q10] What is the primary reason that passing a large struct by value to a function in C can incur a significantly higher performance penalty compared to passing a pointer to the struct?
options: Passing by value implicitly forces the compiler to invoke malloc() behind the scenes to duplicate the struct on the heap.
By-value passing requires copying the entire struct's contents onto the stack, which consumes both memory bandwidth and stack space proportional to the struct's size.
Passing a struct by value causes all its members to be automatically converted to volatile, disabling register allocation.
Pointers can be optimized via tail-call elimination, whereas passing structs by value prevents any function inlining.
questions.correctAnswer: By-value passing requires copying the entire struct's contents onto the stack, which consumes both memory bandwidth and stack space proportional to the struct's size.
questions.explanation: In C, passing an argument by value means the exact contents of that variable or aggregate must be duplicated and placed onto the call stack. For large structures containing many fields, this entails a heavy memory copy overhead (memcpy-like operation) that scales with the size of the structure. Passing a pointer only copies the machine address (typically 4 or 8 bytes), regardless of the structure's size.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to the physical bytes of a structure when it is passed as an argument to a function parameter by value.
questions.relatedConcept: C - Struct passing overhead and call stack mechanics
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand the low-level mechanical cost of abstraction vs. raw performance in systems programming.

questions.question: [C++ • Test 1 • Q1] What distinguishes 'std::unique_ptr' from 'std::shared_ptr' regarding memory and copy semantics?
options: std::unique_ptr uses garbage collection, shared_ptr does not.
std::unique_ptr is strictly non-copyable with single exclusive ownership; std::shared_ptr uses reference counting on a shared control block.
std::unique_ptr cannot be placed in STL containers.
Both have identical copy constructors.
questions.correctAnswer: std::unique_ptr is strictly non-copyable with single exclusive ownership; std::shared_ptr uses reference counting on a shared control block.
questions.explanation: unique_ptr has zero memory overhead (same size as raw pointer). shared_ptr allocates an atomic control block for reference count tracking.
questions.hint: Move-only exclusive ownership vs reference-counted shared ownership.
questions.interviewTip: Prefer std::make_unique and std::make_shared over raw new allocations.

questions.question: [C++ • Test 1 • Q2] In modern C++11+, what is the fundamental purpose of 'std::move()'?
questions.codeSnippet:
std::vector<int> a = {1, 2, 3};
std::vector<int> b = std::move(a);
options: Moves execution to a parallel background thread.
Frees the memory of variable 'a' immediately.
Clones vector 'a' on stack memory.
Unconditionally casts an lvalue to an rvalue reference (&&) to enable ownership transfer without deep copy.
questions.correctAnswer: Unconditionally casts an lvalue to an rvalue reference (&&) to enable ownership transfer without deep copy.
questions.explanation: std::move does not move anything at runtime; it performs a static_cast to rvalue reference so the move constructor steals internal pointers.
questions.hint: Cast to rvalue reference enabling pointer pilfering.
questions.interviewTip: Remember that moved-from objects remain in a valid but unspecified state.

questions.question: [C++ • Test 1 • Q3] How does dynamic polymorphism achieve runtime function dispatch in C++?
options: By re-compiling bytecode on demand.
Through a hidden vptr pointer in the object pointing to the class vtable (array of virtual function pointers).
Through runtime hash table lookup by method name.
Using reflection metadata loaded in Heap.
questions.correctAnswer: Through a hidden vptr pointer in the object pointing to the class vtable (array of virtual function pointers).
questions.explanation: Each polymorphic class generates a vtable. Object instantiation initializes vptr to point to the appropriate class vtable.
questions.hint: vptr inside object points to vtable array of function addresses.
questions.interviewTip: Virtual calls incur a slight pointer indirection cost and prevent some inlining optimizations.

questions.question: [C++ • Test 1 • Q4] What is the exact behavior and safety implication of invoking a member function on a null pointer in C++?
options: It is guaranteed to execute successfully as long as the member function contains no references to the 'this' pointer.
It is undefined behavior according to the C++ standard, even if the member function does not access any non-static data members or 'this'.
It throws a standard 'std::null_pointer_exception' at runtime.
It results in a compile-time error because member functions cannot be invoked through pointers.
questions.correctAnswer: It is undefined behavior according to the C++ standard, even if the member function does not access any non-static data members or 'this'.
questions.explanation: According to the C++ standard (specifically [expr.ref]), dereferencing a null pointer to form a glvalue to evaluate a non-static member function or data member results in undefined behavior. Even if the method doesn't use 'this', forming the implicit 'this' argument from a null pointer triggers UB.
questions.hint: Think about what the standard says regarding dereferencing null pointers to access non-static member functions.
questions.relatedConcept: C++ Object Model and Undefined Behavior
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if candidates understand that language standards often forbid patterns that happen to 'work' on specific compilers or CPU architectures.

questions.question: [C++ • Test 1 • Q5] In C++, what does the explicit specifier on a conversion function template or constructor prevent, and how does it affect copy-list-initialization?
options: It prevents explicit casts like static_cast while allowing implicit conversions in assignment contexts.
It completely disables list-initialization entirely, forcing users to invoke the conversion operator via function call syntax.
It prevents both implicit conversions and explicit copy-list-initialization syntax (like 'T v = {obj};'), allowing only direct-list-initialization and explicit casts.
It has no effect on user-defined conversion operators, only on constructors.
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents both implicit conversions and explicit copy-list-initialization syntax (like 'T v = {obj};'), allowing only direct-list-initialization and explicit casts.
questions.explanation: An explicit conversion operator prevents implicit conversions (such as #2). Furthermore, since C++11/14/20, explicit conversion operators can still be considered for direct-list-initialization, but copy-list-initialization (using the equals sign) will reject them.
questions.hint: Remember the distinction between direct-list-initialization and copy-list-initialization when dealing with explicit conversion operators.
questions.relatedConcept: C++ Explicit Conversion Operators and Initialization Rules
questions.interviewTip: Advanced C++ interviews often delve into the nuances of copy-list-initialization versus direct-list-initialization with explicit specifiers.

questions.question: [C++ • Test 1 • Q6] What is the exact behavior when an exception is thrown from a custom user-defined destructor during stack unwinding caused by another active exception?
options: The second exception is swallowed, and the first exception continues propagating.
Both exceptions are caught sequentially in the nearest catch block.
Undefined behavior occurs, but standard compilers typically ignore the destructor exception.
std::terminate() is called immediately, abruptly terminating the application.
questions.correctAnswer: std::terminate() is called immediately, abruptly terminating the application.
questions.explanation: According to the C++ Standard (specifically [except.terminate]), if an exception is thrown while stack unwinding is already underway (i.e., a destructor throws an exception while another exception is being handled), std::terminate() is invoked immediately, crashing the process.
questions.hint: Think about what happens when an exception escapes a destructor during active unwinding.
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test your understanding of exception safety guarantees and why destructors must be marked noexcept (or handle their own exceptions).

questions.question: [C++ • Test 1 • Q7] In C++, what is the precise lifetime behavior of a temporary object bound to a reference as a function parameter in a nested call expression?
options: The temporary Derived object is destroyed immediately at the semicolon inside getObj(), leaving a dangling reference.
The temporary Derived object's lifetime is extended to the end of the full-expression containing the call to getObj().
The temporary Derived object's lifetime is extended for the duration of the entire enclosing scope.
Reference binding rules prohibit returning a temporary bound to a reference from a function, causing a compilation error.
questions.correctAnswer: The temporary Derived object is destroyed immediately at the semicolon inside getObj(), leaving a dangling reference.
questions.explanation: While binding a temporary object to a reference extends its lifetime to the lifetime of the reference under certain conditions, this extension does NOT apply when returning a reference from a function. The temporary created by `Derived()` is destroyed at the end of the evaluation of the return statement, resulting in a dangling reference when `getObj()` returns.
questions.hint: Check the rules for temporary lifetime extension across function return boundaries.
questions.relatedConcept: Temporary Lifetime Extension and Dangling References
questions.interviewTip: This is a classic trap testing deep comprehension of lifetime extension rules versus function return boundaries.

questions.question: [C++ • Test 1 • Q8] What is the primary compilation-time and performance trade-off introduced by utilizing C++ `constexpr` functions compared to standard runtime functions?
options: They force the compiler to generate separate runtime versions for every possible input argument permutation, bloating the heap.
They eliminate all runtime overhead completely by forcing compile-time evaluation, but can significantly increase compilation times and binary code size if heavily abused.
They disable all aggressive compiler optimizations like loop unrolling because the function must remain pure.
They restrict the function to using only raw pointers, preventing the use of any modern C++ container types at runtime.
questions.correctAnswer: They eliminate all runtime overhead completely by forcing compile-time evaluation, but can significantly increase compilation times and binary code size if heavily abused.
questions.explanation: A `constexpr` function can be evaluated at compile-time if given constant expressions, shifting computation to the build phase to reduce runtime latency. However, excessive or complex compile-time metaprogramming heavily taxes the compiler parser/optimizer, increasing compilation times, and can lead to code bloat if the compiler is forced to emit runtime fallbacks or duplicate logic.
questions.hint: Consider what happens during the build phase when the compiler has to execute complex logic before generating machine code.
questions.relatedConcept: C++ - constexpr and Compile-Time Evaluation Trade-offs
questions.interviewTip: Interviewers use this to test if a candidate understands that performance gains in execution speed via `constexpr` often come at the expense of compile-time latency and potential binary size increases.

questions.question: [Java • Test 1 • Q1] What does the 'volatile' keyword guarantee in Java multithreading?
options: Provides complete synchronized locking on the variable.
Prevents the object from being garbage collected.
Guarantees memory visibility across threads by reading/writing directly to main memory, without providing mutual exclusion/atomicity.
Makes compound operations like count++ atomic.
questions.correctAnswer: Guarantees memory visibility across threads by reading/writing directly to main memory, without providing mutual exclusion/atomicity.
questions.explanation: Volatile prevents CPU caching and instruction reordering for that variable, ensuring changes by one thread are immediately visible to all others.
questions.hint: Visibility guarantee, not atomic locking.
questions.interviewTip: For compound atomic operations, use AtomicInteger / AtomicReference instead of volatile.

questions.question: [Java • Test 1 • Q2] What will be printed by 'System.out.println(s1 == s2);' when 'String s1 = "Java"; String s2 = new String("Java");'?
options: false (s1 references String Constant Pool, s2 references a distinct Heap object).
true (JVM string deduplication merges references).
Compilation Error.
NullPointerException.
questions.correctAnswer: false (s1 references String Constant Pool, s2 references a distinct Heap object).
questions.explanation: == compares object memory addresses. Literal references the String Pool; 'new String()' allocates a separate Heap instance.
questions.hint: Use .equals() for content comparison, == compares references.
questions.interviewTip: Calling s2.intern() returns the pooled canonical reference.

questions.question: [Java • Test 1 • Q3] In Java 8+, what happens when a HashMap bucket collision list reaches 8 elements (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD)?
options: Throws a MaxBucketCollisionException.
Rehashes all keys into a flat array.
The linked list bucket converts into a balanced Red-Black Tree (TreeNode), reducing lookup time to O(log n).
Discards oldest entries via LRU policy.
questions.correctAnswer: The linked list bucket converts into a balanced Red-Black Tree (TreeNode), reducing lookup time to O(log n).
questions.explanation: Java 8 converts linked lists (O(n) worst case) to Red-Black self-balancing trees (O(log n) worst case) once table capacity >= 64 and bucket >= 8.
questions.hint: Linked list treeifies into Red-Black Tree.
questions.interviewTip: Ensure custom keys implement consistent equals() and hashCode() methods.

questions.question: [Python • Test 1 • Q1] What is the primary advantage of using a generator expression '(x*2 for x in data)' over list comprehension '[x*2 for x in data]'?
options: Generators evaluate lazily on-demand using O(1) memory, avoiding allocating the full list in RAM.
Generators execute 100x faster on GPU.
List comprehensions cannot be iterated in for loops.
Generators automatically save output to disk.
questions.correctAnswer: Generators evaluate lazily on-demand using O(1) memory, avoiding allocating the full list in RAM.
questions.explanation: Generators yield items one at a time using iterator protocol, making them essential for processing gigabyte-scale datasets.
questions.hint: Lazy evaluation saves RAM.
questions.interviewTip: Generators are ideal for streaming log files or continuous database cursor streams.

questions.question: [Python • Test 1 • Q2] What is the output of calling 'def fn(val, acc=[]): acc.append(val); return acc' twice with fn(1) then fn(2)?
questions.codeSnippet:
def fn(val, acc=[]):
    acc.append(val)
    return acc
print(fn(1))
print(fn(2))
options: [1] then [2]
[1] then [1, 2] (default list object is bound ONCE at function definition time).
TypeError: default argument modified
questions.correctAnswer: [1] then [1, 2] (default list object is bound ONCE at function definition time).
questions.explanation: Default parameter values are evaluated once when def executes. The same list object is shared across subsequent invocations.
questions.hint: Use 'acc=None' inside function signature to create fresh default lists.
questions.interviewTip: Always use None as default value for mutable arguments in Python.

questions.question: [Python • Test 1 • Q3] How does the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) impact multithreading in CPython?
options: Restricts execution of Python bytecode to a single native thread at a time, limiting CPU-bound speedup across multiple cores.
Prevents memory leaks during asyncio coroutines.
Enforces static types on all global variables.
Bans socket networking over multiple threads.
questions.correctAnswer: Restricts execution of Python bytecode to a single native thread at a time, limiting CPU-bound speedup across multiple cores.
questions.explanation: GIL protects CPython memory management. CPU-bound code requires multiprocessing to achieve true multi-core parallelism.
questions.hint: One thread executes bytecode at a time in CPython.
questions.interviewTip: Use multiprocessing for CPU heavy tasks, threading/asyncio for I/O bound tasks.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q1] Why do database storage engines (InnoDB, Postgres) utilize B+ Trees instead of standard Binary Search Trees?
options: B+ Trees eliminate all disk writes.
Binary trees cannot store string keys.
B+ Trees automatically compress data in RAM.
High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.correctAnswer: High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.explanation: B+ Trees store records only in linked leaves. The wide branching factor (high fan-out) reduces tree height to 3-4 levels for millions of rows.
questions.hint: High fan-out reduces disk page reads.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - B+ Tree Indexing & Range Lookups
questions.interviewTip: Understand covering index (index-only scan) optimization for SQL queries.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q2] What is the primary purpose of the Circuit Breaker pattern in microservice architecture?
options: Encrypts payload traffic with TLS.
Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
Balances network load across all containers.
Compresses JSON responses.
questions.correctAnswer: Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
questions.explanation: Circuit Breakers track failure rates and trip Open to reject requests immediately, returning fallback responses until health recovers.
questions.hint: Fails fast to protect system resilience.
questions.interviewTip: Always define fallbacks and reasonable timeout thresholds for HTTP clients.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q3] What causes Thrashing in Operating System memory management?
options: CPU clock speed throttled due to temperature.
Network sockets buffer overflow.
Deadlock among mutual exclusion locks.
Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.correctAnswer: Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when active working sets exceed physical RAM, causing continuous page faults and disk I/O thrashing.
questions.hint: Continuous page faults and disk swapping.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - OS Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
questions.interviewTip: Working set model prevents thrashing by ensuring processes have sufficient page frames.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q4] What is the sequence of control flags exchanged during the standard TCP connection establishment?
options: ACK -> SYN -> FIN
SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
SYN -> ACK -> DATA
RST -> SYN -> ACK
questions.correctAnswer: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
questions.explanation: Client sends SYN with initial sequence number (ISN), Server responds with SYN-ACK, Client sends ACK to establish full-duplex session.
questions.hint: Synchronize, Synchronize-Acknowledge, Acknowledge.
questions.interviewTip: TCP 3-way handshake sequence is a universal computer network interview question.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q5] In SOLID principles, what does the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) enforce?
options: Every class must inherit from exactly one parent.
Classes should be open for modification and closed for extension.
Dependencies must be hardcoded statically.
Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.correctAnswer: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.explanation: LSP guarantees that derived classes honor the contract and behavior expectations established by the base type.
questions.hint: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - Object Oriented Design & SOLID Principles
questions.interviewTip: Violating LSP often occurs when overriding methods with empty implementations or unexpected exceptions.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q6] In Distributed Storage, how does Consistent Hashing minimize partition migration when a node is added?
options: Rehashes all keys across all servers from scratch.
Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
Duplicates all partitions to every machine in cluster.
Freezes all transactions until rebalancing completes.
questions.correctAnswer: Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
questions.explanation: Consistent Hashing ensures that only adjacent ring segments are redistributed, minimizing network transfer during cluster scaling.
questions.hint: Hash ring bounds key migration to immediate neighbors.
questions.relatedConcept: TypeScript - Consistent Hashing in Distributed Systems
questions.interviewTip: Amazon DynamoDB and Cassandra use consistent hashing with virtual nodes.

questions.question: [TypeScript • Test 1 • Q7] Which SQL transaction isolation level prevents Dirty Reads and Non-Repeatable Reads, but may allow Phantom Reads?
options: READ COMMITTED
READ UNCOMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
REPEATABLE READ
questions.correctAnswer: REPEATABLE READ
questions.explanation: Repeatable Read locks scanned rows preventing updates, but standard SQL allows concurrent transactions to insert new matching rows (phantoms).
questions.hint: Read Uncommitted < Read Committed < Repeatable Read < Serializable.
questions.interviewTip: Serializable eliminates all anomalies via strict range locking or SSI.

questions.question: What is the standard behavior when `longjmp()` is invoked from a nested function call, provided the corresponding `setjmp()` was called in an outer function that has already returned?
options: Undefined behavior, typically resulting in corruption of the call stack or a segmentation fault.
The program cleanly exits with code 1.
It safely resets execution back to the `setjmp` call site inside `outer`.
A compilation error due to stack frame mismatch.
questions.correctAnswer: Undefined behavior, typically resulting in corruption of the call stack or a segmentation fault.
questions.explanation: Invoking `longjmp` after the function that invoked `setjmp` has returned execution destroys the target stack frame context, leading to undefined behavior.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to local stack frames when functions exit.
questions.interviewTip: Always ensure `setjmp` scopes outlive any matching `longjmp` calls.

questions.question: How does the `restrict` keyword, introduced in C99, affect pointer analysis and compiler optimizations?
options: It guarantees that the pointers are the sole initial means of referencing the memory objects they point to within their scope, enabling aggressive load/store optimizations.
It makes the pointers thread-safe by enforcing atomic memory operations.
It restricts pointer arithmetic, preventing out-of-bounds index errors at runtime.
It enforces that the pointer can only be read from and never written to.
questions.correctAnswer: It guarantees that the pointers are the sole initial means of referencing the memory objects they point to within their scope, enabling aggressive load/store optimizations.
questions.explanation: The `restrict` type qualifier tells the compiler that for the lifetime of the pointer, only it (or a derivative) will be used to access the object it points to, allowing the compiler to optimize without worrying about aliasing.
questions.hint: Think about pointer aliasing and how compilers optimize loops and memory access.
questions.interviewTip: Mention alias analysis when discussing performance tuning in C.

questions.question: In the context of C preprocessor macros, what is the primary pitfall of the following macro definition?

It results in multiple evaluations of `x` causing side effects if expressions like `SQUARE(i++)` are used.
Both A and C are correct.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the `volatile` keyword in embedded or concurrent C programming?
options: It prevents the compiler from optimizing out seemingly redundant reads or writes, ensuring every access goes directly to physical memory or hardware registers.
It ensures that the variable is stored in thread-local storage across multiple threads.
It makes operations on the variable atomic without requiring mutex locks.
It protects the memory region from being swapped out to disk.
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents the compiler from optimizing out seemingly redundant reads or writes, ensuring every access goes directly to physical memory or hardware registers.
questions.explanation: `volatile` informs the compiler that the value can be changed by entities outside the control of the program (like hardware or interrupts), disabling memory access optimizations.
questions.hint: Think about memory-mapped I/O and compiler optimization loops.
questions.interviewTip: Remember that `volatile` deals with visibility and optimization, NOT atomicity or thread safety.

questions.question: What does the `sig_atomic_t` type guarantee in signal-handling contexts?
options: Access to objects of type `sig_atomic_t` can be performed atomically, without the possibility of reading or writing half-updated values.
It guarantees that the variable is protected by a hardware-level spinlock.
It forces the compiler to allocate the variable in CPU registers exclusively.
It allows safe execution of multi-threaded thread pools within signal handlers.
questions.correctAnswer: Access to objects of type `sig_atomic_t` can be performed atomically, without the possibility of reading or writing half-updated values.
questions.explanation: `sig_atomic_t` is guaranteed to be read or written in a single uninterrupted operation, making it safe to modify in a signal handler and read in the main program (especially when combined with `volatile`).
questions.hint: Consider interrupt and signal safety when modifying variables shared with signal handlers.
questions.interviewTip: Always mark shared signal flags as `volatile sig_atomic_t`.

questions.question: What is the behavior of the following code snippet regarding pointer arithmetic on `void *`?

questions.interviewTip: To remain strictly portable, always cast `void *` to `char *` before performing arithmetic.

questions.question: What is the behavior of calling `realloc(ptr, 0)` when `ptr` is a valid pointer allocated previously on the heap?
questions.codeSnippet:

ptr = realloc(ptr, 0);
options: It frees the memory pointed to by `ptr` and returns either `NULL` or a unique pointer that can be passed to `free`.

questions.explanation: According to the C standard, passing 0 as the new size to `realloc` is equivalent to calling `free(ptr)`. It may return `NULL` or a pointer that must be freed.

questions.interviewTip: Modern coding guidelines recommend avoiding `realloc(ptr, 0)` for clarity; use explicit `free()` instead.

questions.explanation: Proportional reacts to current error, Integral eliminates accumulated steady-state error, and Derivative dampens rate of error change to prevent overshoot.

questions.interviewTip: Excessive derivative gain amplifies sensor noise in flight controllers.

questions.question: [Operations & Supply Chain • Test 1 • Q8] Why do database storage engines (InnoDB, Postgres) utilize B+ Trees instead of standard Binary Search Trees? (Variant 1.8)
options: B+ Trees eliminate all disk writes.
Binary trees cannot store string keys.
B+ Trees automatically compress data in RAM.
High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.correctAnswer: High fan-out minimizes disk I/O depth (O(log_B N)), and linked leaf nodes allow sequential range scans.
questions.explanation: B+ Trees store records only in linked leaves. The wide branching factor (high fan-out) reduces tree height to 3-4 levels for millions of rows.
questions.hint: High fan-out reduces disk page reads.
questions.relatedConcept: Operations & Supply Chain - B+ Tree Indexing & Range Lookups
questions.interviewTip: Understand covering index (index-only scan) optimization for SQL queries.

questions.question: [Operations & Supply Chain • Test 1 • Q9] What is the primary purpose of the Circuit Breaker pattern in microservice architecture? (Variant 1.9)
options: Encrypts payload traffic with TLS.
Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
Balances network load across all containers.
Compresses JSON responses.
questions.correctAnswer: Fails fast when downstream services become unresponsive, preventing cascading thread starvation across the system.
questions.explanation: Circuit Breakers track failure rates and trip Open to reject requests immediately, returning fallback responses until health recovers.
questions.hint: Fails fast to protect system resilience.
questions.relatedConcept: Operations & Supply Chain - Microservices Circuit Breaker Pattern
questions.interviewTip: Always define fallbacks and reasonable timeout thresholds for HTTP clients.

questions.question: [Operations & Supply Chain • Test 1 • Q10] What causes Thrashing in Operating System memory management? (Variant 1.10)
options: CPU clock speed throttled due to temperature.
Network sockets buffer overflow.
Deadlock among mutual exclusion locks.
Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.correctAnswer: Main memory is overloaded, causing the OS to spend more time swapping pages to disk than executing process instructions.
questions.explanation: Thrashing occurs when active working sets exceed physical RAM, causing continuous page faults and disk I/O thrashing.
questions.hint: Continuous page faults and disk swapping.
questions.relatedConcept: Operations & Supply Chain - OS Virtual Memory & Page Replacement
questions.interviewTip: Working set model prevents thrashing by ensuring processes have sufficient page frames.

questions.question: [Operations & Supply Chain • Test 1 • Q11] What is the sequence of control flags exchanged during the standard TCP connection establishment? (Variant 1.11)
options: ACK -> SYN -> FIN
SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
SYN -> ACK -> DATA
RST -> SYN -> ACK
questions.correctAnswer: SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK
questions.explanation: Client sends SYN with initial sequence number (ISN), Server responds with SYN-ACK, Client sends ACK to establish full-duplex session.
questions.hint: Synchronize, Synchronize-Acknowledge, Acknowledge.
questions.relatedConcept: Operations & Supply Chain - TCP 3-Way Handshake & Flow Control

questions.question: [Operations & Supply Chain • Test 1 • Q12] In SOLID principles, what does the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) enforce? (Variant 1.12)
options: Every class must inherit from exactly one parent.
Classes should be open for modification and closed for extension.
Dependencies must be hardcoded statically.
Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.correctAnswer: Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without altering program correctness.
questions.explanation: LSP guarantees that derived classes honor the contract and behavior expectations established by the base type.
questions.hint: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.
questions.relatedConcept: Operations & Supply Chain - Object Oriented Design & SOLID Principles
questions.interviewTip: Violating LSP often occurs when overriding methods with empty implementations or unexpected exceptions.

questions.question: [Operations & Supply Chain • Test 1 • Q13] In Distributed Storage, how does Consistent Hashing minimize partition migration when a node is added? (Variant 1.13)
options: Rehashes all keys across all servers from scratch.
Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
Duplicates all partitions to every machine in cluster.
Freezes all transactions until rebalancing completes.
questions.correctAnswer: Maps servers and keys to a 360-degree hash ring, so adding a node only migrates k/N keys from its immediate neighbor.
questions.explanation: Consistent Hashing ensures that only adjacent ring segments are redistributed, minimizing network transfer during cluster scaling.
questions.hint: Hash ring bounds key migration to immediate neighbors.
questions.relatedConcept: Operations & Supply Chain - Consistent Hashing in Distributed Systems
questions.interviewTip: Amazon DynamoDB and Cassandra use consistent hashing with virtual nodes.

questions.question: [Operations & Supply Chain • Test 1 • Q14] Which SQL transaction isolation level prevents Dirty Reads and Non-Repeatable Reads, but may allow Phantom Reads? (Variant 1.14)
options: READ COMMITTED
READ UNCOMMITTED
SERIALIZABLE
REPEATABLE READ
questions.correctAnswer: REPEATABLE READ
questions.explanation: Repeatable Read locks scanned rows preventing updates, but standard SQL allows concurrent transactions to insert new matching rows (phantoms).
questions.hint: Read Uncommitted < Read Committed < Repeatable Read < Serializable.
questions.relatedConcept: Operations & Supply Chain - ACID Isolation & Concurrency Anomalies
questions.interviewTip: Serializable eliminates all anomalies via strict range locking or SSI.

questions.question: [AutoCAD • Test 1 • Q1] In automotive design, how does aerodynamic drag force (F_drag) scale with vehicle forward speed (v)?
options: Linear scaling: drag force doubles when speed doubles.
Quadratic scaling: drag force is proportional to the square of vehicle velocity (v^2).
Logarithmic scaling: drag plateaus above 60 mph.
Independent of speed: depends only on vehicle weight.
questions.correctAnswer: Quadratic scaling: drag force is proportional to the square of vehicle velocity (v^2).
questions.explanation: Drag equation F = 0.5 * rho * v^2 * Cd * A. Because speed is squared, doubling vehicle speed quadruples aerodynamic drag force and octuples power required.
questions.hint: Drag force scales with v^2; power scales with v^3.
questions.interviewTip: Streamlined shapes (low Cd) significantly extend highway range for electric vehicles.

questions.question: [AutoCAD • Test 1 • Q2] In civil structural engineering, why is steel reinforcement embedded in the bottom zone of a simply supported concrete beam?
options: Steel reduces the self-weight of the concrete beam.
Steel prevents moisture from entering the aggregate.
Concrete expands 10x more than steel under thermal loads.
Concrete has high compressive strength but very weak tensile strength; steel handles tensile stresses developed at the bottom fibers.
questions.correctAnswer: Concrete has high compressive strength but very weak tensile strength; steel handles tensile stresses developed at the bottom fibers.
questions.explanation: A simply supported beam experiences compression on top and tension on bottom. Rebar provides ductile tensile capacity to prevent brittle failure.
questions.hint: Concrete resists compression; steel resists tension.
questions.relatedConcept: AutoCAD - Reinforced Concrete & Bar Bending Schedule
questions.interviewTip: Concrete and mild steel share nearly identical thermal expansion coefficients (~12 x 10^-6 / °C).

questions.question: [AutoCAD • Test 1 • Q3] In mechanical manufacturing drawings, what does the True Position tolerance symbol specify?
options: The maximum allowable roughness of a machined surface.
Defines a theoretical exact zone within which the center, axis, or center plane of a feature is permitted to vary from its datum.
The hardness rating of the metal alloy.
The tensile strength limit before plastic deformation.
questions.correctAnswer: Defines a theoretical exact zone within which the center, axis, or center plane of a feature is permitted to vary from its datum.
questions.explanation: True position controls location and orientation relative to datums, providing cylindrical tolerance zones that maximize manufacturing acceptance rates.
questions.hint: Exact theoretical location tolerance zone.
questions.interviewTip: GD&T avoids tight coordinate tolerances and facilitates interchangeable parts.

questions.question: [AutoCAD • Test 1 • Q4] How does an electric vehicle (EV/HEV) capture kinetic energy during deceleration?
options: Friction brake pads compress piezoelectric quartz crystals.
Exhaust turbines harvest hot gas pressure during braking.
The transmission shifts into high gear to accelerate the flywheel.
The electric traction motor operates as a generator, converting vehicle momentum into electrical energy that recharges the traction battery pack.
questions.correctAnswer: The electric traction motor operates as a generator, converting vehicle momentum into electrical energy that recharges the traction battery pack.
questions.explanation: Regenerative braking switches the inverter firing sequence so counter-electromotive force slows wheels while rectifying current into the high-voltage pack.
questions.hint: Electric motor functions as a generator during braking.
questions.interviewTip: Regenerative braking reduces mechanical brake pad wear by over 70%.

questions.question: [Psychology (Health Science) • Test 1 • Q1] In nanomedicine and oncology, what is the Enhanced Permeability and Retention (EPR) effect?
options: Nanoparticles dissolve exclusively in stomach hydrochloric acid.
Magnetic fields pull nanoparticles across healthy cell membranes.
Nanoparticles enter cells by destroying lipid bilayers irreversibly.
Nanoparticles preferentially accumulate in tumor tissues due to leaky, hyperpermeable tumor vasculature and defective lymphatic drainage.
questions.correctAnswer: Nanoparticles preferentially accumulate in tumor tissues due to leaky, hyperpermeable tumor vasculature and defective lymphatic drainage.
questions.explanation: Rapid tumor angiogenesis creates fenestrated blood vessels allowing 20-200 nm nanocarriers to extravasate into tumor parenchyma passively.
questions.hint: Leaky tumor blood vessels + poor lymphatic drainage = passive accumulation.
questions.relatedConcept: Psychology (Health Science) - Nanoparticle Targeted Drug Delivery (EPR Effect)
questions.interviewTip: Pegylation of nanoparticles extends blood circulation half-life by evading reticuloendothelial clearance.

questions.question: [Psychology (Health Science) • Test 1 • Q2] In psychological assessment and CBT, what characterizes the cognitive distortion known as 'Catastrophizing'?
options: Attributing success entirely to one's own innate talent.
Anticipating the absolute worst-case scenario and viewing it as unbearable, despite objective evidence suggesting it is unlikely.
Remembering past events with selective positive nostalgia.
Refusing to accept negative emotional states as valid.
questions.correctAnswer: Anticipating the absolute worst-case scenario and viewing it as unbearable, despite objective evidence suggesting it is unlikely.
questions.explanation: Catastrophizing exaggerates potential negative outcomes, fueling anxiety and depressive spirals. Cognitive restructuring reframes these automatic thoughts.
questions.hint: Predicting worst-case scenarios without proportional evidence.
questions.relatedConcept: Psychology (Health Science) - Cognitive Distortions in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
questions.interviewTip: Decatastrophizing exercises ask: 'What is the most likely realistic outcome?'

questions.question: [Psychology (Health Science) • Test 1 • Q3] In genetic engineering, what is the prerequisite for the Cas9 endonuclease to bind and cleave target double-stranded DNA?
options: A reverse transcriptase enzyme bound to the ribosome.
Complete absence of ATP in the nucleus.
Target DNA must be fully methylated.
Presence of a short Protospacer Adjacent Motif (PAM) sequence adjacent to the target guide RNA binding site.
questions.correctAnswer: Presence of a short Protospacer Adjacent Motif (PAM) sequence adjacent to the target guide RNA binding site.
questions.explanation: Cas9 interrogates DNA by first recognizing the PAM sequence (typically 5'-NGG-3' for SpCas9) before unwinding DNA and pairing with the guide RNA.
questions.hint: PAM sequence recognition is required for Cas9 cleavage.
questions.relatedConcept: Psychology (Health Science) - CRISPR-Cas9 Mechanism & PAM Sequence
questions.interviewTip: Engineered Cas variants target alternative PAM sequences to expand genome editing versatility.

Evaluate safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and determine maximum tolerated dose (MTD) in a small group of healthy volunteers.
Post-marketing surveillance and rare adverse event reporting (Phase IV).
Synthesize chemical compounds in laboratory test tubes.
questions.correctAnswer: Evaluate safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and determine maximum tolerated dose (MTD) in a small group of healthy volunteers.
questions.explanation: Phase I tests safety/dose (20-100 participants), Phase II evaluates preliminary efficacy and side effects, Phase III confirms therapeutic benefit at scale.
questions.hint: Phase I = Safety, dosage, and pharmacokinetics.
questions.relatedConcept: Psychology (Health Science) - Clinical Trial Phases & Objectives
questions.interviewTip: Adherence to ICH-GCP guidelines is mandatory across all clinical phases.

questions.question: [UI/UX (Design) • Test 1 • Q1] In digital product design, what is the primary benefit of established typographic scales (Type Scale)?
options: Minimizes the download size of TTF font files.
Prevents CSS layout reflows on mobile devices.
Creates distinct visual hierarchy that guides scanning eyes from primary titles to metadata efficiently.
Enforces monochromatic color palettes across all screens.

questions.question: [UI/UX (Design) • Test 1 • Q2] What does Fitts's Law predict about user interaction with on-screen target elements?
options: The time required to rapidly move to a target is a function of the ratio between distance to the target and width of the target.
Users can hold at most 7 items in short-term memory (Miller's Law).
Decision time increases logarithmically with number of choices (Hick's Law).
Users perceive objects close together as belonging to the same group.
questions.correctAnswer: The time required to rapidly move to a target is a function of the ratio between distance to the target and width of the target.
questions.explanation: Fitts's law dictates that primary call-to-action buttons should be larger and closer to the user's cursor/thumb reach zone.
questions.hint: Target size and distance dictate acquisition time.
questions.relatedConcept: UI/UX (Design) - Fitts's Law in Interface Usability
questions.interviewTip: Screen corners and edges have infinite theoretical width because cursor cannot overshoot them.

questions.question: [UI/UX (Design) • Test 1 • Q6] According to Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.1 AA), what is the minimum contrast ratio required for standard body text? (Variant 1.6)
options: 4.5:1 against its background (3:1 for large text >= 18pt or bold >= 14pt).
2.0:1 for all text elements.
7:1 for all text (this is AAA level).
10:1 strictly across dark mode interfaces.
questions.correctAnswer: 4.5:1 against its background (3:1 for large text >= 18pt or bold >= 14pt).
questions.explanation: WCAG AA compliance mandates at least 4.5:1 contrast for normal text to ensure readability for users with moderate visual impairments.
questions.hint: 4.5:1 for standard text; 3:1 for large text.
questions.interviewTip: Never rely on color alone to convey error states or interactive affordances.
